---
title: "Identifying near-duplicate survey responses: full-distribution matching with false discovery control"
author: "Andrew P. Wheeler"
abstract: |
  A common screen for fraudulent or duplicated survey responses flags any
  pair of respondents whose answers agree above a fixed percentage, such as
  85%. That threshold ignores how many response categories each question has
  and how skewed their marginal distributions are, so it can flag most of a
  survey by chance alone or miss deliberate duplication entirely, depending
  on the instrument. I instead model the full distribution of pairwise match
  counts across every respondent pair, fit an overdispersed null directly to
  the data, and flag outliers with a false discovery rate correction chosen
  for the strong dependence created by comparing every respondent against
  every other respondent. Simulations show the approach avoids false alarms
  from skewed marginals, recovers deliberately duplicated rows when only a
  few fields are altered, and loses power as more fields are changed, which
  is an inherent limit of exact-match comparison rather than a defect of the
  correction. Applied to a real municipal survey, it flags a small number of
  near-duplicate clusters, most explained by long runs of an identical
  Likert response rather than fraud. Code, paper source, and a reproducible
  environment are at https://github.com/apwheele/SurveyMatch.

```{python}
#| label: setup
import matplotlib
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from IPython.display import Markdown

from surveymatch import (
    connected_components,
    expected_match_probs,
    fdr_flag,
    fit_beta_binomial_ml,
    fit_normal_approx,
    match_pvalues,
    null_fit_sse,
    pair_index,
    pairwise_match_counts,
    plot_match_fit,
    simulate_correlated_responses,
    simulate_responses,
)
from surveymatch.matching import poisson_binomial_null

andy_theme = {
    "axes.grid": True,
    "grid.linestyle": "--",
    "legend.framealpha": 1,
    "legend.facecolor": "white",
    "legend.shadow": True,
    "legend.fontsize": 11,
    "legend.title_fontsize": 12,
    "xtick.labelsize": 11,
    "ytick.labelsize": 11,
    "axes.labelsize": 12,
    "axes.titlesize": 13,
    "axes.titlelocation": "left",
    "figure.dpi": 150,
}
matplotlib.rcParams.update(andy_theme)

# Marginal distributions used throughout: a fair coin, and three increasingly
# skewed categorical distributions in which one response dominates. These
# reappear in the simulated examples below.
skew_components = [
    np.array([0.9, 0.1]),
    np.array([75.0, 4.0, 3.0, 2.0, 1.0]),
    np.array([200.0, 20.0] + [3.0] * 8),
]
skew_components = [p / p.sum() for p in skew_components]
```

```{python}
#| label: sim1-setup
rng1 = np.random.default_rng([1])
n1, v1 = 1000, 100
sd1 = simulate_responses(n1, [[0.5, 0.5]] * v1, rng=rng1)
co1 = pairwise_match_counts(sd1)
bb1 = fit_beta_binomial_ml(co1, v1)
pb1 = poisson_binomial_null(expected_match_probs(sd1))
pvals1 = match_pvalues(co1, bb1)
rej1, q1 = fdr_flag(pvals1, alpha=0.05, method="fdr_bh")
```

```{python}
rng2 = np.random.default_rng([2])
n2, v2 = 1000, 100

    skew_components[rng2.integers(len(skew_components))] for _ in range(v2)
]

naive_threshold2 = 0.85 * v2
naive_flagged2 = int((co2 >= naive_threshold2).sum())
bb2 = fit_beta_binomial_ml(co2, v2)
```

```{python}
#| label: sim3-setup
def inject_manipulated_duplicates(base, n_manip, k_manip, rng):
    n_total, v = base.shape
    subcopy = base[:n_manip].copy()
    cols = rng.choice(v, size=k_manip, replace=False)
    for r in range(n_manip):
        for c in cols:
            alt = np.setdiff1d(np.unique(base[:, c]), subcopy[r, c])
            if alt.size:
                subcopy[r, c] = rng.choice(alt)
    out = base.copy()
    out[-n_manip:] = subcopy
    true_pairs = {tuple(sorted((i, n_total - n_manip + i))) for i in range(n_manip)}
    return out, true_pairs


def power_curve_rep(base, n_manip, k_manip, rng, alpha=0.05):
    v = base.shape[1]
    data, true_pairs = inject_manipulated_duplicates(base, n_manip, k_manip, rng)
    counts = pairwise_match_counts(data)
    null_dist = fit_beta_binomial_ml(counts, v)
    pvals = match_pvalues(counts, null_dist)
    rejected, _ = fdr_flag(pvals, alpha=alpha, method="fdr_bh")
    flagged = {
        tuple(sorted(p)) for p in pair_index(data.shape[0], rejected).tolist()
    }
    true_pos = len(true_pairs & flagged)
    false_pos = len(flagged - true_pairs)
    power = true_pos / n_manip
    fdp = false_pos / len(flagged) if flagged else 0.0
    return power, fdp


rng3_base = np.random.default_rng([3, 0])
n3, v3, n_manip3 = 300, 60, 30
base3_probs = [
    skew_components[rng3_base.integers(len(skew_components))] for _ in range(v3)
]
base3 = simulate_responses(n3, base3_probs, rng=rng3_base)

k_grid3 = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 12, 20, 30]
reps3 = 12
power_rows = []
for k in k_grid3:
    powers, fdps = [], []
    for rep in range(reps3):
        rng_rep = np.random.default_rng([3, k, rep])
        power, fdp = power_curve_rep(base3, n_manip3, k, rng_rep)
        powers.append(power)
        fdps.append(fdp)
    power_rows.append({"k_manip": k, "power": np.mean(powers), "fdp": np.mean(fdps)})
power_df = pd.DataFrame(power_rows)
```

```{python}
#| label: fdr-calibration-setup
n4, v4 = 250, 25
rho_grid4 = [0.0, 0.3, 0.5]
reps4 = 50
calib_rows = []
for rho in rho_grid4:
    any_bh, n_bh, any_by, n_by = [], [], [], []
    for rep in range(reps4):
        rng_rep = np.random.default_rng([4, int(rho * 10), rep])
        data = simulate_correlated_responses(
            n4,
            v4,
            category_probs=[0.7, 0.2, 0.1],
            tilt=[1.0, -0.3, -0.7],
            rho=rho,
            rng=rng_rep,
        )
        counts = pairwise_match_counts(data)
        null_dist = fit_beta_binomial_ml(counts, v4)
        pvals = match_pvalues(counts, null_dist)
        rej_bh, _ = fdr_flag(pvals, alpha=0.05, method="fdr_bh")
        rej_by, _ = fdr_flag(pvals, alpha=0.05, method="fdr_by")
        any_bh.append(rej_bh.sum() > 0)
        n_bh.append(rej_bh.sum())
        any_by.append(rej_by.sum() > 0)
        n_by.append(rej_by.sum())
    calib_rows.append(
        {
            "rho": rho,
            "bh_p_any": np.mean(any_bh),
            "bh_mean_n": np.mean(n_bh),
            "by_p_any": np.mean(any_by),
            "by_mean_n": np.mean(n_by),
        }
    )
calib_df = pd.DataFrame(calib_rows)
```

```{python}
#| label: real-data-setup
survey_raw = pd.read_csv("data/raleigh_survey_2018.csv")
item_cols = list(survey_raw.columns)[4:68]
survey_items = survey_raw[item_cols].fillna(9).astype(int).to_numpy().clip(1, 9)
n5, v5 = survey_items.shape
co5 = pairwise_match_counts(survey_items)
bb5 = fit_beta_binomial_ml(co5, v5)
nm5 = fit_normal_approx(co5)
sse_bb5 = null_fit_sse(co5, bb5, v5)
sse_nm5 = null_fit_sse(co5, nm5, v5)
use_normal5 = sse_nm5 < sse_bb5
chosen_null5 = nm5 if use_normal5 else bb5
chosen_name5 = "normal" if use_normal5 else "beta-binomial"
pvals5 = match_pvalues(co5, chosen_null5)
rej5, q5 = fdr_flag(pvals5, alpha=0.05, method="fdr_by")
flagged_pairs5 = pair_index(n5, rej5)
components5 = connected_components(flagged_pairs5) if flagged_pairs5.size else []
components5 = sorted(components5, key=len, reverse=True)


def component_summary(rows):
    sub = survey_items[rows]
    unanimous_items = int(sum(len(np.unique(sub[:, c])) == 1 for c in range(v5)))
    vals, cnts = np.unique(sub, return_counts=True)
    modal_value = int(vals[np.argmax(cnts)])
    modal_share = cnts.max() / sub.size
    return unanimous_items, modal_value, modal_share


component_rows = []
for i, rows in enumerate(components5, start=1):
    unanimous_items, modal_value, modal_share = component_summary(rows)
    component_rows.append(
        {
            "component": i,
            "n_respondents": len(rows),
            "unanimous_items": unanimous_items,
            "modal_value": modal_value,
            "modal_share": modal_share,
        }
    )
component_df = pd.DataFrame(component_rows)
```

# Introduction

Survey researchers routinely need to flag suspicious duplicate responses: a
paper respondent whose form was scanned twice, a web panelist replaying the
same session, or a data-entry error that copied one row into another.
@kuriakose2016 proposed a simple screen for this: compute the percentage of
questions on which each pair of respondents gave an identical answer, and
flag any pair above 85%. @pewresearch2016 and @day2023trustissues each point
out the same problem with a fixed threshold: how often two independent,
honest respondents agree by chance depends entirely on how the response
categories are distributed, not on any threshold that generalizes across
surveys. A battery of Likert items dominated by a few common answers can put
the *large majority* of pairs above 85% agreement with no duplication at
all, while a survey with many balanced, high-cardinality items will rarely
reach that rate even for a genuine copy.

This paper develops a full-distribution alternative. Rather than comparing
each pair's match percentage to a fixed cutoff, I estimate the distribution
of match counts across every pair of respondents in the survey and flag
pairs that are outliers relative to that fitted distribution. Because every
respondent takes part in $n-1$ comparisons, the resulting test statistics are
highly dependent, so the multiple-comparisons correction needs to tolerate
that dependence rather than assume independent tests. I also analyze the
*entire* set of pairwise comparisons rather than each respondent's single
largest match: reducing the problem to one extreme value per respondent
needlessly complicates the analysis and can miss a respondent who was copied
into several near-duplicates rather than just one.

The method is a screening tool, not a fraud determination. A flagged pair is
a candidate for follow-up review, and the paper's real-data example shows
that most flagged clusters have an ordinary explanation -- a respondent who
gave the same Likert response to nearly every item. The contribution is
calibration: knowing which pairs are actually unusual, given the survey's own
response distributions, rather than applying a rule of thumb that was
calibrated on a different survey with different marginals.

# Related work

@kuriakose2016 is the starting point for this literature: a fixed
percentage-match rule intended to flag fabricated survey data. @pewresearch2016
critiqued the rule using Pew's own cross-national surveys, showing that many
genuine respondent pairs exceed 85% agreement simply because several items
have highly skewed response distributions. @day2023trustissues independently
reached the same conclusion auditing a university's own survey data, and both
critiques motivate the approach here: model the actual distribution of
matches for the survey at hand instead of importing a threshold from another
one.

The method is also distinct from probabilistic record linkage
[@fellegisunter1969; @enamorado2019], which weights field-by-field agreement
by how informative each field is and is normally used to merge or de-duplicate
records *across* separate files where true matches are rare and fields are
a mix of continuous and categorical types. Here every respondent answers the
same fixed categorical instrument, matches are compared within a single
fielded survey, and the goal is to characterize the entire distribution of
agreement rather than to score one-off candidate matches.

Comparing response *patterns* also appears in test-fraud detection.
@jacoblevitt2003 flag classrooms with unusual within-classroom agreement on
blocks of answers, including agreement on wrong answers, which is a stronger
signal than agreement alone but requires an answer key that a general opinion
survey does not have. Fabricated data can also be detected by
non-content forensic cues -- sorting artifacts, implausible formatting --
as in @datacolada2023, and web-panel administrators can use paradata such as
IP addresses and timestamps [@urbaninstitute2023] that are unavailable for
a paper instrument like the one analyzed in this paper. Response-content
matching is a complementary signal to all of these, useful precisely when
paradata and answer keys are not available.

The mean number of matches two independent respondents share on a single
question is the sum of squared response-category proportions, i.e. the
complement of the Gini--Simpson diversity index [@simpson1949]. Skewed
marginals mechanically inflate this quantity, which is the mathematical root
of the miscalibration problem described above. Finally, because comparing
every respondent to every other respondent produces $\binom{n}{2}$ dependent
test statistics, the relevant correction is a false discovery rate procedure
that tolerates dependent tests [@benjaminihochberg1995; @benjaminiyekutieli2001],
discussed further below.

# Method

## Setup

Each of $n$ respondents answers $v$ categorical questions. Question $c$ has
$K_c$ response categories with population proportions $p_{c1},\dots,p_{cK_c}$.
For a pair of respondents $i \neq j$, define the match count

$$
M_{ij} = \sum_{c=1}^v \mathbb{1}\{X_{ic} = X_{jc}\},
$$

the number of questions on which they gave the identical answer. The method
compares every one of the $\binom{n}{2}$ values of $M_{ij}$ to a fitted null
distribution, rather than thresholding $M_{ij}/v$ against a fixed rate.

## Expected matches under independence

For two respondents drawn independently from the population, the probability
they match on question $c$ depends only on that question's marginal
distribution:

$$
\theta_c = \Pr(X_{ic}=X_{jc}) = \sum_{k=1}^{K_c} p_{ck}^2.
$$

Summing over questions gives the expected total match count,
$\mu=\sum_c \theta_c = E[M_{ij}]$, exactly, with no assumption about
correlation between questions *within* a respondent. That correlation instead
determines $\mathrm{Var}(M_{ij})$: correlated answers make the per-question
match indicators correlated for a given pair, inflating the variance of
$M_{ij}$ above what independence would imply while leaving its mean
unchanged. This is the mechanism behind @sec-sim2 below -- a handful of
dominant response categories can push $\mu$ itself above a naive 85%
threshold, with no need for any correlation or duplication at all.

If the $v$ questions were independent given respondent identity, $M_{ij}$
would follow a Poisson-binomial distribution with success probabilities
$\theta_1,\dots,\theta_v$, computable exactly by a standard $O(v^2)$
convolution recursion (implemented in `poisson_binomial_null`). Real survey
items are rarely independent within a respondent -- response styles,
acquiescence, and genuinely correlated attitudes all push several items in
the same direction for the same person -- so this exact null understates
$\mathrm{Var}(M_{ij})$ for real data. It remains useful as a check: when
questions really are independent, as in the simulation of @sec-sim1, the
Poisson-binomial and an empirically fit null should agree closely.

## An empirically fit null

Rather than assume independence, I fit an overdispersed distribution
directly to the observed $\binom{n}{2}$ match counts. The primary choice is a
beta-binomial, $M \sim \mathrm{BetaBinomial}(v,\alpha,\beta)$, fit by maximum
likelihood. A closed-form method-of-moments estimator exists but is unstable
near the boundary of valid $(\alpha,\beta)$; direct likelihood maximization is
used throughout (`fit_beta_binomial_ml`). When match counts are
*under*-dispersed relative to a binomial -- rare in practice, since it
implies a survey with less pairwise agreement than independent chance would
produce -- the method-of-moments algebra returns an invalid negative
$\alpha$ or $\beta$, in which case a normal approximation matched to the
sample mean and standard deviation is used instead
(`fit_normal_approx`). The real-data application in this paper also uses the
normal approximation, chosen automatically because it fits the observed
histogram better than the beta-binomial's maximum-likelihood fit (measured by
sum of squared error against the empirical histogram, `null_fit_sse`); see
@sec-realdata.

Given a fitted null $\hat F$, each pair receives a one-sided p-value,
$p_{ij} = \Pr(M \ge m_{ij}) = 1-\hat F(m_{ij}-1)$, evaluated here as
$1-\hat F(m_{ij})$ for a slightly conservative discrete convention.

## Multiple comparisons under dependence

Testing all $\binom{n}{2}$ pairs is a large multiple-comparisons problem, and
the tests are not independent: every respondent appears in $n-1$ of them, so
a respondent with an unusually common response profile inflates several
$p_{ij}$ at once. The Benjamini--Hochberg procedure [@benjaminihochberg1995]
controls the false discovery rate under independence or positive regression
dependence, while the Benjamini--Yekutieli procedure [@benjaminiyekutieli2001]
controls it under arbitrary dependence at the cost of being more
conservative. @sec-calibration checks both empirically and finds that
Benjamini--Hochberg is already somewhat liberal purely from
respondent-sharing, even with independent questions, and that its excess
false-flag rate grows sharply once questions are also correlated within a
respondent. Benjamini--Yekutieli is better calibrated throughout that range,
though its protection is not unconditional either -- at strong enough item
correlation both procedures break down together. This motivates using
Benjamini--Yekutieli as the safer default, and specifically for the real,
correlated survey data in @sec-realdata.

## Grouping flagged pairs

Flagging pairs rather than respondents means one respondent's row can appear
in several flagged pairs -- for instance if it was the source of a copy that
was then further altered. I therefore treat the flagged pairs as edges of a
graph and extract its connected components (`connected_components`), which
groups respondents into clusters of mutual near-duplication rather than
forcing an analyst to reassemble that structure from a flat pair list.

# Simulated examples

## Baseline calibration {#sec-sim1}

As a first check, I replicate @kuriakose2016's original simulation:
`{python} f"{n1:,}"` respondents answer `{python} f"{v1}"` independent,
evenly split yes/no questions. @fig-sim1 compares the observed distribution
of the `{python} f"{len(co1):,}"` pairwise match counts against the
maximum-likelihood beta-binomial fit. Because the questions are genuinely
independent here, the fitted beta-binomial mean
(`{python} f"{bb1.mean():.1f}"`) and variance
(`{python} f"{bb1.var():.2f}"`) closely track the exact Poisson-binomial
null's mean (`{python} f"{pb1.mean():.1f}"`) and variance
(`{python} f"{pb1.var():.2f}"`), confirming the empirical fit recovers the
right answer when the textbook independence assumption actually holds. At a
5% false discovery rate, Benjamini--Hochberg flags
`{python} f"{int(rej1.sum())}"` pair(s) out of
`{python} f"{len(co1):,}"` -- consistent with testing this many true nulls at
that error rate, not evidence of any real duplication.

```{python}
#| label: fig-sim1
#| fig-cap: "Sim 1: replication of the KR baseline (1,000 respondents, 100 independent Bernoulli(0.5) questions). Bars are the observed proportion of pairs at each match count; the line is the maximum-likelihood beta-binomial fit."
plot_match_fit(co1, bb1, v1)
plt.show()
```

## Skewed marginals: a red herring {#sec-sim2}

A fixed match-rate threshold implicitly assumes every survey produces about
the same chance agreement rate. @fig-sim2 shows a simple counter-example: the
same number of respondents and questions as @sec-sim1, but each question is
now drawn from one of three skewed distributions with a single dominant
response category (as could arise from a battery of Likert items with strong
ceiling effects). No duplication or manipulation is introduced anywhere.
Summing the per-question collision probabilities gives an expected match
rate of `{python} f"{mu2/v2*100:.0f}%"` of all `{python} f"{v2}"` questions --
already close to the 85% rule-of-thumb threshold from chance alone. In the
simulated sample, `{python} f"{naive_flagged2:,}"` of the
`{python} f"{len(co2):,}"` pairs (`{python} f"{naive_flagged2/len(co2)*100:.1f}%"`)
exceed the naive 85% match rate, which a fixed-threshold rule would flag as
suspicious. The calibrated approach instead fits the null to this survey's
own marginals and flags `{python} f"{int(rej2.sum())}"` pairs at a 5% false
discovery rate, correctly finding nothing unusual.

```{python}
#| label: fig-sim2
#| fig-cap: "Sim 2: skewed marginals with no duplication. Each of 100 questions is drawn from one of three distributions with a single dominant response category. The observed distribution (bars) and beta-binomial fit (line) both sit well above what an 85%-of-questions rule-of-thumb (dashed) would treat as normal."
ax = plot_match_fit(co2, bb2, v2)
ax.axvline(naive_threshold2, color="firebrick", linestyle=":", label="85% threshold")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.show()
```

## Detecting manipulated duplicates {#sec-sim3}

The scenario the method is actually meant to catch is deliberate but lazy
duplication: copying an existing response and changing a handful of fields.
Starting from a skewed-marginal population like @sec-sim2 (`{python} f"{n3}"`
respondents, `{python} f"{v3}"` questions), I copy `{python} f"{n_manip3}"`
rows, randomly alter $k$ of the $v_3$ fields in each copy, and check whether
the true copy-original pairs are recovered. @fig-sim3-power shows detection
power -- the fraction of the `{python} f"{n_manip3}"` true duplicate pairs
correctly flagged -- and the false discovery proportion among flagged pairs,
averaged over `{python} f"{reps3}"` replications at each value of $k$. Power
is high when only a few fields are altered and falls as $k$ grows, which is
an unavoidable property of exact-field matching rather than a weakness of the
correction: once enough fields differ, a manipulated copy is no longer
statistically distinguishable from an independent respondent who happens to
share the same skewed marginals. The false discovery proportion stays
controlled near the nominal 5% level throughout, so the method does not
compensate for lost power by flagging more false positives.

```{python}
#| label: fig-sim3-power
#| fig-cap: "Sim 3: detection power and false discovery proportion for a 30-row manipulated duplicate batch, as a function of how many of 60 fields were altered per copy. Each point averages 12 replications."
fig, ax1 = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.2))
ax1.plot(power_df["k_manip"], power_df["power"], marker="o", color="black", label="Power")
ax1.plot(power_df["k_manip"], power_df["fdp"], marker="s", color="firebrick", label="False discovery proportion")
ax1.axhline(0.05, color="grey", linestyle=":", linewidth=1)
ax1.set_xlabel("Number of fields altered per manipulated copy ($k$)")
ax1.set_ylabel("Proportion")
ax1.set_ylim(-0.02, 1.02)
ax1.legend(frameon=False)
plt.show()
```

## Choosing an FDR procedure under correlated items {#sec-calibration}

@sec-sim1 and @sec-sim2 use independent questions, but that alone does not
make the $\binom{n}{2}$ pairwise tests independent of each other: every
respondent contributes to $n-1$ of them, which is enough dependence by
itself to matter. @tbl-bhby simulates `{python} f"{n4}"` respondents on
`{python} f"{v4}"` questions whose answers share a common respondent-level
trait of increasing strength $\rho$ (so $\rho=0$ isolates pure
respondent-sharing dependence, and larger $\rho$ adds real within-respondent
item correlation on top of it), with the beta-binomial null re-fit to each
simulated sample and no true duplicates present. Because no true duplicates
exist, any rejection is a false one, so the proportion of replications with
at least one rejection is directly comparable to the nominal 5% level. Even
at $\rho=0$, Benjamini--Hochberg's false-rejection rate
(`{python} f"{calib_df.loc[calib_df.rho == 0.0, 'bh_p_any'].iloc[0]*100:.0f}%"`)
sits well above 5% from respondent-sharing alone, while Benjamini--Yekutieli
stays near or below it
(`{python} f"{calib_df.loc[calib_df.rho == 0.0, 'by_p_any'].iloc[0]*100:.0f}%"`).
As $\rho$ increases, Benjamini--Hochberg's excess grows sharply while
Benjamini--Yekutieli remains better calibrated over most of this range --
though at the highest correlation shown, both procedures flag nearly every
replication, which is a reminder that no multiple-comparisons correction can
fully compensate for a badly misspecified single overall null once
respondents cluster into strongly self-similar subgroups. This is why
@sec-realdata below uses Benjamini--Yekutieli for the real, correlated
survey data.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bhby
#| tbl-cap: "Empirical false-rejection rate under the true null (no duplicates) as within-respondent item correlation increases. 'P(any rejection)' is the share of 50 replications with at least one flagged pair; a well-calibrated procedure at the 5% level should keep this at or below 0.05."
display_df = calib_df.rename(
    columns={
        "rho": "Correlation (rho)",
        "bh_p_any": "BH: P(any rejection)",
        "bh_mean_n": "BH: mean # flagged",
        "by_p_any": "BY: P(any rejection)",
        "by_mean_n": "BY: mean # flagged",
    }
)
Markdown(display_df.to_markdown(index=False, floatfmt=(".2f", ".3f", ".2f", ".3f", ".2f")))
```

# Application: the 2018 Raleigh community survey {#sec-realdata}

I apply the method to a public block of `{python} f"{v5}"` Likert-style items
from the City of Raleigh's 2018 community survey
(`{python} f"{n5:,}"` respondents; see the `data/` folder for the source file
and codebook). Response categories are collapsed to the integers 1--9,
following the source instrument's coding, with missing values coded 9. This
is real fielded data, not a simulation, so I do not know the ground truth of
which pairs, if any, are genuine duplicates.

The beta-binomial maximum-likelihood fit visibly underestimates the left
skew of the observed match-count distribution for this survey; the automatic
goodness-of-fit check confirms the normal approximation is the better fit
(sum of squared error `{python} f"{sse_nm5:.5f}"` vs.
`{python} f"{sse_bb5:.5f}"`), so the normal null is used here, exactly as the
method's fallback rule anticipates. @fig-real-fit shows both fits for
comparison. At a 5% false discovery rate with the Benjamini--Yekutieli
correction, `{python} f"{int(rej5.sum())}"` of the
`{python} f"{len(co5):,}"` pairs are flagged, forming
`{python} f"{len(components5)}"` connected components of mutually
near-duplicate respondents.

```{python}
#| label: fig-real-fit
#| fig-cap: "Observed pairwise match-count distribution for the Raleigh survey (64 items) against maximum-likelihood beta-binomial and normal-approximation fits. The normal fit is used for the flagging analysis because it has lower sum of squared error against the histogram."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 4), sharey=True)
plot_match_fit(co5, bb5, v5, ax=axes[0], label="Beta-binomial")
axes[0].set_title("Beta-binomial fit")
plot_match_fit(co5, nm5, v5, ax=axes[1], label="Normal", color="firebrick")
axes[1].set_title("Normal fit")
axes[1].set_ylabel("")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

@tbl-components summarizes the flagged clusters. For each, "unanimous items"
counts how many of the 64 questions every respondent in the cluster answered
identically, and "modal share" is the fraction of all cell values in the
cluster equal to its single most common value. Clusters with both figures
high are consistent with a respondent giving one repeated response to most
of the survey -- a long "run" of, say, all 5's -- rather than a copied and
lightly edited record. Clusters with lower values on both measures have more
varied response patterns and are comparatively harder to explain by a single
repeated response.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-components
#| tbl-cap: "Connected components of flagged near-duplicate pairs in the Raleigh survey. Unanimous items counts questions where every respondent in the cluster gave the identical answer; modal share is the fraction of all cell values equal to the cluster's single most common value."
display_components = component_df.rename(
    columns={
        "component": "Component",
        "n_respondents": "Respondents",
        "unanimous_items": "Unanimous items (of 64)",
        "modal_value": "Modal value",
        "modal_share": "Modal share",
    }
)
Markdown(display_components.to_markdown(index=False, floatfmt=(".0f", ".0f", ".0f", ".0f", ".2f")))
```

Most components have a high count of unanimous items and a high modal share,
consistent with respondents who gave the same Likert response -- most often
a 4, 5, or the missing-data code 9 -- across nearly the entire instrument;
duplicate flags here most plausibly reflect straight-lining rather than
copied records. The remaining components have more varied responses across
their unanimous items and a lower modal share, and are correspondingly
harder to write off; they are the pairs an analyst reviewing this survey
would want to look at individually.

# Discussion

The central point is that "unusual" is relative to a survey's own response
distributions, not a fixed percentage borrowed from a different instrument.
Fitting the null directly avoids two opposite failure modes: treating
ordinary skewed-marginal agreement as fraud, and letting a genuinely
suspicious pattern slide because it falls under an arbitrary cutoff. Testing
every pairwise comparison, rather than only the maximum match per
respondent, also lets the method surface a respondent duplicated into
several near-copies -- a pattern a single-comparison approach would only
partially recover.

The simulations also show a real limit of the method, not just its
strengths: recovery power depends almost entirely on how many fields a
manipulator bothered to change, and beyond a modest number of altered fields
a deliberately manipulated row is statistically indistinguishable from an
independent respondent. This screen is therefore best understood as catching
lazy duplication and unintentional retakes, not a determined adversary who is
willing to edit most of the record. That is a reasonable division of labor:
someone who can systematically and plausibly fabricate an entire response
profile is better caught by other means, such as paradata or field
experience, not by post-hoc statistical screening of the response content
alone [@urbaninstitute2023].

The false discovery rate correction matters as much as the null model.
@sec-calibration shows that even with a correctly fit marginal null,
treating the $\binom{n}{2}$ pairwise tests as independent understates the
false-flag rate, because every respondent contributes to $n-1$ tests at
once; that gap widens sharply once survey items are also realistically
correlated within a respondent. Benjamini--Yekutieli's guarantee under
arbitrary dependence is a
conservative fix; a useful extension would be a dependence-aware resampling
or permutation-based procedure calibrated to a specific survey's actual item
correlation structure, which could recover some of the power that
Benjamini--Yekutieli gives up.

Finally, this is a screening tool. A flagged cluster in @sec-realdata is a
candidate for an analyst's review, not proof of a bad-faith response, and the
majority of the flagged clusters in that example are well explained by a
respondent repeating one answer through most of a long instrument. The value
of the method is in directing that review efficiently and consistently,
rather than by a rule of thumb that changes meaning from one survey to the
next.
